# The Kilogram That Couldn't Be Wrong

For 130 years, the kilogram was a particular object. It was a cylinder of platinum-iridium alloy, 39 millimeters tall and 39 across, a little shorter than a golf ball. It was cast in London in 1879 and kept in a vault in Sèvres, just outside Paris, under three nested glass bell jars. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. From 1889 until 2019, this cylinder was not a very good measurement of the kilogram. It *was* the kilogram, and everything else in the world that had mass had it in relation to this one piece of metal.

The odd consequence is that the cylinder could not be wrong. If a careless technician had scratched off a speck of metal, the cylinder would still have weighed exactly one kilogram, by definition. In the bookkeeping of science, everything else in the universe would have become slightly heavier.

And something like that seems to have happened. The prototype had official copies, six stored alongside it and dozens more distributed to national laboratories. About every forty years the copies came back to Sèvres to be compared with the original. By the third comparison, around 1990, the copies and the original had drifted apart by roughly 50 micrograms on average, about the mass of a grain of fine sand. The copies appeared to have gained mass, which may mean the prototype had lost some. Nobody knows which, and under the old definition the question had no answer. Proposed explanations included gas trapped in the metal at casting and slowly escaping, and contaminants accumulating on the surfaces at different rates. The official cleaning procedure, incidentally, was to rub the cylinder by hand with a chamois soaked in ether and alcohol, then rinse it with a jet of steam.

Fifty micrograms in a kilogram is five parts in a hundred million, and nobody buying flour cares. But the kilogram sat underneath other units. The newton is defined through it, and so are the joule, the watt, and, by a chain of definitions, the volt and the ampere. By the late twentieth century, physicists could make electrical measurements with more precision than the mass standard those measurements ultimately rested on. Some of the most refined experiments ever built were limited by a Victorian metal cylinder that was doing something unexplained in a basement.

What makes this more than a technical annoyance is that the metric system was founded to avoid exactly this situation. The French revolutionaries who designed it wanted units that belonged to no king and no country, "for all time, for all people," in Condorcet's phrase. So the meter was to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and the kilogram the mass of a liter of water. Nature itself would be the standard, and anyone could consult it. But the Earth is hard to survey and water is hard to weigh precisely, so in practice they made a metal bar and a metal weight to embody the results. The artifacts were then more convenient and more reproducible than the natural quantities they stood for, and they became the definitions. The universal system ended up locked in a vault in a Paris suburb.

The meter escaped first. In 1960 it was redefined by a wavelength of light from krypton atoms, and in 1983 by the distance light travels in a fixed fraction of a second. The second was tied to a frequency of the cesium atom. One by one the units were detached from objects and attached to constants, until the kilogram was the last unit still defined by a thing you could drop.

Mass is hard to tie to a constant, and the eventual fix took decades. The key instrument was invented in 1975 by Bryan Kibble, a British physicist. It is a balance that weighs an object against an electromagnetic force rather than against another object. The current and voltage that produce the force can be measured using quantum effects, and those effects connect to Planck's constant, the number that sets the scale of quantum mechanics. Planck's constant has units that include the kilogram, the meter, and the second. Since the meter and second were already fixed, pinning Planck's constant to an exact value pins down the kilogram too.

Getting the instruments good enough took until the 2010s. In November 2018, delegates from dozens of countries met in Versailles and voted to make the change, and on May 20, 2019, it took effect. Planck's constant is now exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, with no uncertainty, forever. The value was chosen so that the new kilogram matched the old one as closely as anyone could measure, and nobody's bathroom scale changed.

The part I keep thinking about is the inversion. Before 2019, the cylinder was exact and Planck's constant was a measured quantity with error bars. Afterward, the constant was exact and the cylinder became an ordinary object whose mass is approximately one kilogram, give or take some micrograms, to be determined by experiment. After 130 years of being right by definition, it can now be wrong, and it can be weighed to find out how wrong. Whether it was the prototype or the copies that drifted is now a question with an answer.

The change also redeems the revolutionary promise, at least on paper. In principle, a laboratory anywhere can now realize the kilogram from scratch, without sending anything to France. Even a laboratory on another planet could. In practice, a Kibble balance costs millions and only a handful exist, so most of the world still gets its kilogram through a chain of metal weights compared against other metal weights, leading back to a few national labs. The standard is now universal in a way that almost nobody can use directly. That seems like a fair description of a lot of universal things.

Kibble died in 2016, two years before the vote, and his device, long called the watt balance, was renamed the Kibble balance in his honor. The cylinder is still in its vault in Sèvres, still under its three bell jars. It was not thrown out, and metrologists plan to keep weighing it over the coming decades.

I'm deciding on a topic for the 1000-word piece and weighing a few options, like pencils, maps, tides, or the word "thing." I'm leaning toward desire paths, the dirt trails people wear across lawns, and I'm starting to think through that idea.

I'm weighing the kilogram as a topic too: the International Prototype Kilogram, which lost about 50 micrograms against its copies and was retired in 2019 in favor of a definition fixed by Planck's constant. The core question is whether defining a unit by a physical object versus a constant changes what it means for the unit to be "wrong."

I'm checking the kilogram's recalibration history: copies drifted from the prototype by about 50 micrograms over a century, roughly a grain of fine sand, and since the prototype is the definition, there's no way to tell which side moved. I'm also noting the 2018 vote, the 2019 switch to a fixed Planck constant, and the Kibble balance and silicon-sphere projects that made that switch possible.

I'm working out the kilogram's original definition, a litre of water at the ice point, and the meter's history, from a quadrant survey through Paris to a platinum bar and then a wavelength of krypton light. The kilogram stands out as the last unit still pinned to a physical artifact.

I'm settling on the kilogram's history for the piece: a platinum-iridium cylinder kept near Paris that defined mass for over a century, and the way its copies drifted from it. I'm also planning to end on something concrete rather than a neat closing line.

I'm picturing the object itself now: a platinum-iridium cylinder roughly as tall as a golf ball, cast in London in 1879 and kept in a vault outside Paris under nested bell jars, where three different people had to hold keys to open it.

I'm noting that the copies were compared against the prototype three times over the century, and by the third check around 1990 they'd come out about 50 micrograms heavier on average. There's no way to tell whether the copies gained mass or the prototype lost it, since the prototype is the reference. I'm also considering contamination and hydrogen released from the metal as possible causes.

I'm moving on to the idea that the revolutionaries wanted units meant for all people and all times, with the metre taken from the Earth and the kilogram tied to water. Water proved hard to pin down, so they settled on a metal artifact, and the artifact ended up as the definition. The metre got free of its object in 1960 and again in 1983, which left the kilogram as the last one still tied to a physical thing.

I'm now considering the kilogram's shift from object to constant: the cylinder in Sèvres used to be exact by definition while Planck's constant was measured with uncertainty, and that has flipped. The old cylinder now has an uncertainty of its own, and it can finally be wrong. Any well-equipped lab could in principle realize the unit, though Kibble balances are expensive and few exist.

I'm reaching the ending now: the cylinder still sitting in its vault under the bell jars, and the note that Bryan Kibble died in 2016, two years before the vote, with his balance named after him. I want to finish on a concrete image rather than a tidy line.
